scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is in their early 20s, living with parents due to pandemic housing issues, and just had a work meeting where their parents' argument was visible on camera. Now they're being blamed for "filming a private family matter" and kicked out. They're asking if they're the asshole (AITA) for this situation.

First, I need to analyze the dynamics here. The key points: 
- The user has no control over the meeting setup ( dining room with no door, open to hallway)
- Parents' arguments are " normalized" for them due to long-term dysfunction
- They explicitly told coworkers about their family situation before
- When the argument happened, they handled it calmly: "Hold on, can you still hear me?... coffee break"
- Only after parents started screaming in view of camera did they ask them to " keep it down"
- Dad saw himself on camera and got angry, then both parents blamed the user for " filming private matter" even though the user wasn't recording them intentionally

Hmm... the core issue seems to be about responsibility for the exposure. Let me mentally simulate the scenario: 
- User is in a work meeting with colleagues who already know their family dynamics 
- Parents walk into a shared space (hallway visible to camera) during a screaming match 
- User didn't intentionally point camera at them; it's just that the room has no door 
- When they noticed, they tried to de-escalate by pausing the meeting 
- Only after that did they ask parents to lower voices 

...Wait, the parents are the ones who chose to argue in a public space (hallway adjacent to where user is working). The user didn't " film" them - the meeting camera was on for work purposes, and the parents' own actions brought them into frame. 

*Pausing to consider societal norms* 
- In most workplaces, it's understood that home environments can have background noise. 
- Colleague's prior knowledge of family situation means they'd likely not be shocked 
- The user's response was professional: " coffee break" to handle the situation 
- Parents' reaction is disproportionate - they're angry at the user for their own behavior being visible 

*Checking for user's responsibility* 
- Did the user intentionally record them? No 
- Did the user set up the camera to capture them? No 
- Was the room designed for privacy? No ( " no door" ) 
- Did the user provoke the argument? No 
- Did the user handle it appropriately? Yes ( pausing meeting, calmly asking for quiet ) 

*父母的视角* 
- They might feel exposed, but... 
- They chose to argue in a space where work was happening 
- They're adults - they should know to avoid public arguments 
- Blaming the user for their own actions is... not logical 

*Final judgment* 
- The user did nothing wrong 
- Parents are the ones who created the situation by arguing in a shared space 
- " Filming a private matter" is a mischaracterization - the user wasn't filming them; they were in frame incidentally 
- Kicking the user out over this is extreme and unfair 

*Additional angles* 
- The user has a lease starting next month - this is temporary 
- Parents' " apology" demand is about their own shame, not the user's fault 
- If anything, the parents should apologize for creating the disruption 

*Conclusion* 
- Not the asshole (NTA) 
- The parents are the ones acting unreasonably here 
- User's only " mistake" was not having a closed door, but that's not their fault ( they're living there, not the homeowner) 

*Why this matters* 
- This is about boundaries: parents should respect the user's work space 
- Blaming the victim is toxic - the user didn't cause the argument 
- The " AITA" framing is misleading because the user's actions were entirely appropriate 

*Final answer* 
- 0 (NTA) 
- Because the user did nothing wrong; the parents' behavior caused the issue, and their reaction is disproportionate
